content.title: Is Sean Miller already Texas' greatest basketball coach?
content.text: SAN JOSE, Calif. — While I got ya, here are nine things and one crazy prediction: 1. A potential GOAT He’s been on campus just 12 months. But by the time he leaves Texas, Sean Miller will be the best Longhorn basketball coach in history. Unless, of course, he caps his team’s improbable run and wins the school’s first men’s basketball national championship this year and gets hired away by somebody like North Carolina or Kansas or Kentucky. Don’t think bluebloods wouldn’t come sniffing around Austin to grab the Miller magic. I’ll be stunned if Hubert Davis remains coach of the Tar Heels. I expect Bill Self to retire after his extreme heart problems and Jacque Vaughn to succeed him. I don’t think Mark Pope has a long leash with the Wildcats, although I’m betting he survives for another season at least. But would Miller even want that rat race if any of them wanted him? Pressure at Texas is not the same as those other three spots, unless your name is Steve Sarkisian. … A case could be made that if Texas beats Purdue on Thursday to reach the Elite Eight for the fifth time in his career, Miller would be an easy choice for national coach of the year. As it is, he should already be a contender for that honor by taking an 11th seed to the Sweet 16. … As for being the best ever at Texas, I understand it’s a very small sample size with one full year not even being in the books yet. Now some of you may agree with me. Others might say balderdash and think no way. I have a soft spot for Rick Barnes, whom I consider a dear friend. He elevated Texas basketball with his consistency and regular NBA talent like no other and kept it nationally prominent, but he is so defensive-minded, and Miller offers more balance. The flamboyant Tom Penders completely resurrected the sport from the Bob Weltlich era and made Texas basketball fun and lively with the Runnin’ Horns. Both those coaches are legends at Texas but didn’t win a natty. Neither has Miller yet. Abe Lemons won an NIT and always filled reporters’ notebooks with colorful and outlandish quotes in between puffs on his ever-present cigar. Leon Black integrated the sport at Texas. But Miller is an elite X’s-and-O’s coach, a master of in-game adjustment and someone who can mobilize the talent he has and bring out the best of it. One national observer said, “Sean’s incredibly calm. That spills over to his players. And he always gets the ball in the hands of his playmakers.” He also said he doesn’t think Miller would leave Austin because he’s grateful for Texas taking a shot on a 57-year-old coach whose career was in doubt after the troubled situation in Arizona. And he might not want the pressure cooker of a North Carolina or Kentucky if they even called, anyway. Also the sign of a great coach is molding your personnel to a winning system than forcing the system. Or as Bum Phillips once said about Bear Bryant, “He can take his’n and beat your’n, and then he can take your’n and beat his’n.” To me, that sums up Sean Miller, whose team is the only double-digit seed still alive in the tournament. … The good news for Texas is that Chris Del Conte and Kevin Eltife keep making exceptional hires. The bad news is they have to keep giving them bonuses and extensions to keep them. Del Conte declined to address the issue Tuesday. Miller signed a six-year, $32 million guaranteed contract last May, which includes a $6 million buyout that drops to $5 million if he leaves after March 31, annual salary increases and up to $850,000 in yearly performance bonuses, so he’s not hurting for dough. His annual salary goes up from $4.8 million — which was 14th nationally but just seventh highest in the SEC — to $5 million next season. … Of course, Texas’ men and women have helped fill the league’s coffers by earning for the SEC $4.5 million already because all men's teams get $2 million for their conference for every game they play (the First Four doesn't count) and the women's teams get $250,000 per game. Both have reached the Sweet 16. 2. Road warriors This Texas basketball team deserves so much credit and applause for getting off the mat and taking advantage of an opportunity very few considered. To lose five of six games and turn around and win three straight in the NCAA Tournament is nothing short of spectacular. … And consider this. All three games were virtually road games. Totally. The Longhorns won at Dayton’s UD Arena where the entire joint was immersed in Miller hate over the Dayton-Xavier rivalry and reigned boos upon him and former Musketeer Dailyn Swain and supported North Carolina State. The Longhorns won at Moda Center with 11,000-plus screaming for the BYU Cougars. The Longhorns won another at Spokane Southwest as Gonzaga fans filled the gym. But that only served to motivate these Longhorns. Essentially all three were road wins with small pockets of maybe 200 burnt orange fans sprinkled around the stands. … Texas had an unremarkable 4-6 record in true road games this season, 4-7 if you count the loss to Duke in neighboring Charlotte. The Longhorns started SEC play a depressing 1-4, beating only Alabama on the road. Maybe San Jose will be kinder to the Longhorns this week since Purdue is even further away than Texas. But I doubt it. … Texas will again be without backup center Lassina Traore, who will miss his 13th straight game with knee soreness. Nor has he been traveling with the team although Miller insisted there’s nothing sinister about his absence. “We were just hoping the knee could progress, and it just hasn’t,” Miller said. “For a while there, it just made a lot of sense academically, and also just his rehab. No reason to travel and not be able to do (rehab). While he’s at home, he’s able to really work. So no, but I don’t think it’ll progress to that. We just progressed so much since then, it’s been so long. I don’t think it can happen.” Nic Codie has more than filled his role, however, and might find himself on the court alongside Matas Vokietaitis against a tall Purdue team although Traore did get 14 rebounds in a game this year. 3. Lackawhat? The Texas women started strong with two landslide wins, but the never satisfied Vic Schaefer smartly found room for improvement with his Longhorns’ 11 turnovers and general “lackadaisical-ness,” even after disposing of Missouri State and Oregon with 42-point wins. Ever the perfectionist, Schaefer is always chasing the perfect game, and he knows the attention to the smallest of details can make the difference in winning it all and coming up short again. He knows how to push the right buttons and has his deepest and most talented Longhorn team ever and now catches fifth-seeded Kentucky (25-10), a team Texas beat by 11 this season. … If Madison Booker keeps playing at this level, scoring a career-best 40 last game, can anyone stop the Longhorns? “Madison is as beautiful as baller as we’ve seen,” said Texas executive senior associate athletic director Chris Plonsky, who’s been on hand to watch women’s basketball for 38 years. 4. Saving the best for last? Should Jim Schlossnagle move Dylan Volantis from Game 3 starter to closer, the role that made him an All-American? I don’t imagine the Longhorn head coach would seriously consider such a drastic move with a series against Oklahoma this week, but it does make a little sense. Now that Texas has already blown two big ninth-inning leads in SEC games against Ole Miss and Auburn and fell to 2-2 before winning Game Two against the Tigers in a nail-biter, it is food for thought. And freshman Sam Cozart could probably slide into that No. 3 starting spot and do well. But it would be a gamble, and Volantis would probably prefer to remain a starter for his long-range goals. Starters make a lot more money than closers. Schlossnagle told the Houston Chronicle that such a switch is not on the table. “We still believe we have the guys down there to finish games,” he said Tuesday.  “Volantis won’t be moved for the foreseeable future.” That said, Burns pitched out of a bases-loaded jam in the ninth inning in Game 2 against Auburn after loading the bases with a walk and two hit batters in the ninth of Game 1 against Ole Miss and blew the save. … Adrian Rodriguez relatively speaking is struggling with the bat in his ongoing recovery from hand surgery in the offseason, his batting average falling to .280, just seventh best on the team. The driven sophomore shortstop dealt with it most of last season and has been slow to move on from it. Asked about Rodriguez’s health, Schlossnagle said, “I would say Adrian is about 60% but he’s healing. It’s just slower than anyone wants. He’s the most courageous player I’ve ever coached, and everyone needs to be grateful for what he’s doing.” Amen to that. He’s a legit gamer. … His situation and the season-ending loss of outfielder Jonah Williams to shoulder surgery deprives Texas of two big bats — well, 1½ to be more accurate — in a powerful lineup that is very thin on positional player depth. That has made the huge, surprising contributions from freshman Anthony Pack Jr. and role player Jayden Duplantier all the more valuable. Sign up for Kirk Bohls' new newsletter for news, exclusive analysis and insights on University of Texas sports. 5. Things I think I know I think I know the Astros will make the playoffs. …… I think I know some will argue the near-upsets of Siena over Duke, Santa Clara over Kentucky, Furman over UConn and High Point over Arkansas means the NCAA Tournament should expand the field to 76, and I couldn’t argue against that. However, no mid-major made it to the Sweet 16 round for the second straight year. … I think March Madness is as mad as ever. What a superb first week for college basketball. … If you’re not playing the squares game where random numbers are assigned and players get the last digits of the winning and losing teams, you’re missing out. My buddy, Cedric Golden won three squares in the first three days of the tournament. … I think this is a huge spring for Longhorns like receiver and bowl game standout Kaliq Lockett, safety Derek Williams Jr., edge rusher Brad Spence and Michigan State tight transfer Michael Masunas, who has 24 career catches. Or was until Lockett suffered a leg injury and will sit out the rest of the spring. … I think I wish flag football was not an Olympic sport. What’s next, rock, paper or scissors? … I think Western Kentucky offensive lineman Laurence Seymore gaining eligibility for the upcoming season is the biggest news of the spring for Steve Sarkisian. “We’re trying to become an experienced group up front.” Sarkisian said. “We had lived in a world where we were so experienced for so long, and last year, we felt inexperienced at times and I thought that it showed.” So did the rest of us. … I think Portland is a fantastic city with the cleanest, prettiest and quietest airport I’ve ever been in, with terrific restaurants like Ox and Grits ’n’ Gravy and the Cajun tater tots at The Independent sports bar with cool architecture and neat vibe. Wish I’d stopped in Voodoo Doughnuts. … I think the AL and NL MVPs are Baltimore shortstop Gunnar Henderson over Kansas City shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. and Atlanta outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. over Cincinnati’s Elly De La Cruz. Where’s the fun in picking Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani? I’d also put Toronto’s Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber in that mix. … I’ve got Boston’s Garrett Crochet and the Pirates’ Paul Skenes as Cy Young Award winners. And Guardians outfielder Chase DeLauter (over Houston’s Tatsuya Imai and Reds first baseman Sal Stewart (barely over Pirates phenom Konnor Griffin since he’s starting in the minor leagues for a minute or two). 6. Can’t beat a good buzzer beater How big was the biggest in Week One? Could Otega Oweh’s near half-court, 32-foot buzzer beater — a banker, no less — for Kentucky be as famous and memorable as Christian Laettner’s turnaround jumper for Duke to beat Kentucky in 1992? Probably even though it only tied Santa Clara and sent the game into overtime that the Wildcats won. It will certainly be up there for Big Blue fans forever. … I know Texas fans will never forget Cam Heide’s clutch 3-pointer from the corner with 14 seconds left to seal the win over Gonzaga even though Matas Vokietaitis’ final runout dunk will distort the significance of Heide’s heave slightly because it made the final margin a wider 74-68. … Shots like those are what fans live for. I’ve been lucky enough to see in person Heide’s shot as well as Mario Chalmers’ famous 3 in San Antonio and Razorback U.S. Reed’s half-court, 47-foot game-winner to beat defending national champion Louisville in 1981 at the Erwin Center and a whole bunch of killer shots by Tramon Mark to beat Texas A&M twice and North Carolina State and BYU and the list goes on. … Oweh’s dagger — is it still a dagger since it didn’t win the game; maybe more of a very deep paper cut — should rank right up there with Villanova’s Kris Jenkins’ trey to beat North Carolina; the 16-foot jumper by some freshman named Michael Jordan to top Georgetown although Craig Ehlo remembers a more memorable MJ shot; Danny Ainge’s coast-to-coast layup to stun Notre Dame; and Chalmers’ 3 over Memphis’ Derrick Rose for Kansas except that it tied the game that the Jayhawks won in overtime in the Alamodome. … Vanderbilt’s desperation heave by Tyler Tanner would have qualified as well if it didn’t have so much juice on the shot and angrily spun out of the rim to give Nebraska a reprieve. Hey, the Cornhuskers deserve a little good luck that never having won an NCAA Tournament game until two days before against Troy. All of those breathtaking shots are so much more impressive than, uh, Lorenzo Charles’ easy dunk of an airball shot for sixth-seeded North Carolina State in 1983, heartbreaking though it was for Houston fans. … As Heide told us in that jubilant Texas locker room, he’d rehearsed shots just like that when he was 13 years old and playing brother Keaton on the sport court his dad built in the backyard in Wayzata, Minn. Still a kid’s game, and it’s beautiful. 7. Scatterbrained Cam Skattebo made a boo-boo recently when he dismissed the serious consequences of CTE and called it “an excuse.” Thankfully, the New York Giants running back apologized profusely for his “tasteless joke” and backtracked on the deadly neurodegenerative disease, which claimed the lives of players like Junior Seau, Conrad Dobler, Dave Duerson and so many others. A Boston University study in 2023 discovered that evidence of CTE was found in 92% of the NFL players whose brains that were donated for the survey. Skattebo also called asthma “fake.” As one of the 262 million people worldwide who have battled asthma all their lives, I can assure you it is not. About as fake as a dislocated ankle, Cam. 8. Scattershooting While wondering whatever happened to former 7-foot Longhorn center Chris Mihm. 9. On the couch Have any of you seen “Death by Lightning”? It’s a terrific, well-written mini-series on Netflix about the assassination of President James Garfield. The shame of it is that it is only four episodes. Wish it had been twice that. Matthew Macfayden, who was excellent as Tom in the wildly successful “Succession,” plays the disgruntled, mentally challenged, fame-seeking character who literally kills it as Charles Guiteau, Garfield’s assassin. Michael Shannon plays the lead role to perfection as does Nick Offerman as the bumbling, drunkard vice president who inherits the office. A must-see show. Gave it 9 ducks. Crazy prediction I’d be glad to take credit for predicting last week that one No. 1 seed would get upset before the Sweet 16 round except for the fact that I also predicted Florida would win it all. Oops. I now predict Texas’ Dailyn Swain turns pro this year.
